questions.text: He is capable ____ solving this complex problem.
questions.explanation: The adjective "capable" is idiomatically followed by the preposition "of".

questions.text: She was absorbed ____ reading her novel.
questions.explanation: "Absorbed in" means deeply engaged in an activity.

questions.text: The teacher was angry ____ the noisy students.
questions.explanation: One is "angry with" a person, but "angry at" a thing or situation.

questions.text: He is anxious ____ his son's health.
questions.explanation: "Anxious about" expresses worry concerning something; "anxious for" means eager for something.

questions.text: The results were contrary ____ our expectations.
questions.explanation: "Contrary to" is the fixed idiomatic preposition used with this adjective.

questions.text: This book consists ____ ten chapters.
questions.explanation: "Consist of" means to be made up of.

questions.text: He succeeded ____ passing the entrance examination.
questions.explanation: "Succeed in" doing something is the standard idiom.

questions.text: The candidate is eligible ____ the post of assistant director.
questions.explanation: "Eligible for" a post or position is the correct collocation.

questions.text: The children were engaged ____ a lively debate.
questions.explanation: "Engaged in" is used for taking part in an activity.

questions.text: The old man leaned ____ the wall to rest.
questions.explanation: "Lean against" means to rest one's weight on a surface.

questions.text: He was involved ____ a financial scandal.
questions.explanation: "Involved in" describes participation in an event or activity.

questions.text: The soldiers fought bravely ____ the invading army.
questions.explanation: "Fight against" an enemy denotes opposition.

questions.text: He is closely related ____ the finance minister.
questions.explanation: "Related to" indicates a family or kinship connection.

questions.text: This company deals ____ imported machinery.
questions.explanation: "Deal in" refers to trading a particular type of goods.

questions.text: The professor is well versed ____ ancient history.
questions.explanation: "Versed in" means knowledgeable or skilled in a subject.

questions.text: She ____ her work by 6 pm tomorrow.
questions.explanation: The future perfect tense expresses an action that will be completed before a specified future time.

questions.text: They ____ football when it suddenly started raining.
questions.explanation: The past continuous describes an action in progress when another action interrupted it.

questions.text: I ____ Multan before last year; this was my first visit.
questions.explanation: The past perfect is used for an action completed before another stated point in the past.

questions.text: He ____ in this bank for ten years now.
questions.explanation: The present perfect continuous shows an action that began in the past and continues now, with emphasis on duration.

questions.text: By next year, she ____ her degree.
questions.explanation: The future perfect tense is used for an action that will be finished before a stated future point.

questions.text: The sun ____ in the east.
questions.explanation: A universal or permanent truth is expressed in the simple present tense.

questions.text: While I ____ dinner, the doorbell rang.
questions.explanation: The past continuous describes an ongoing action interrupted by a shorter past action.

questions.text: She ____ her assignment yet; she needs another hour.
questions.explanation: "Yet" with an unfinished action calls for the present perfect negative.

questions.text: If I ____ you, I would apologise to her immediately.
questions.explanation: The subjunctive "were" is used for hypothetical situations in a second conditional, regardless of the subject.

questions.text: He ____ before we arrived at the station; the train had already gone.
questions.explanation: The past perfect shows an action completed before another past action, here our arrival.

questions.text: The labourers ____ overtime for a week when the strike was suddenly called off.
questions.explanation: The past perfect continuous emphasises the duration of an action that had been ongoing before another past event.

questions.text: I ____ this report since nine o'clock this morning.
questions.explanation: The present perfect continuous is used for an action that started in the past and is still continuing, with duration stated.

questions.text: The flight ____ at nine o'clock tomorrow morning, according to the schedule.
questions.explanation: The simple present tense is used for a fixed, scheduled future event such as a timetable.

questions.text: She always ____ about her heavy workload, which annoys her colleagues.
questions.explanation: The present continuous with "always" expresses a habitual, often irritating, action.

questions.text: Unless you ____ now, you will miss the last train.
questions.explanation: In conditional clauses beginning with "unless", the simple present is used to refer to future time.

questions.text: The doctor suggested that she ____ more rest.
questions.explanation: The base form "take" is used in the subjunctive mood after verbs of suggestion such as "suggest".

questions.text: I would rather you ____ him about the plan just yet.
questions.explanation: "Would rather" followed by a different subject takes a past-tense (subjunctive) verb, even though the meaning is present or future.

questions.text: No sooner ____ he arrived than it began to rain heavily.
questions.explanation: "No sooner... than" requires the past perfect tense in the first clause.

questions.text: Scarcely ____ the film begun when the electricity failed.
questions.explanation: "Scarcely... when" also requires the past perfect tense.

questions.text: By the time the police arrived, the thieves ____ the building.
questions.explanation: The past perfect tense shows an action completed before another past action, here the police arriving.

questions.text: Choose the correct passive voice: 'She writes a letter every day.'
options: A letter was written by her every day.
A letter is being written by her every day.
A letter has been written by her every day.
A letter is written by her every day.
questions.explanation: The simple present passive is formed with is/am/are plus the past participle.

questions.text: Choose the correct passive voice: 'The police arrested the thief.'
options: The thief was arrested by the police.
The thief is arrested by the police.
The thief has been arrested by the police.
The thief had been arrested by the police.
questions.explanation: A simple past active sentence becomes simple past passive: was/were plus the past participle.

questions.text: Choose the correct passive voice: 'They will complete the project next month.'
options: The project will be completed by them next month.
The project is completed by them next month.
The project would be completed by them next month.
questions.explanation: Simple future active becomes "will be + past participle" in the passive.

questions.text: Choose the correct passive voice: 'She is cooking dinner.'
options: Dinner was being cooked by her.
Dinner is being cooked by her.
Dinner has been cooked by her.
questions.explanation: The present continuous passive is formed with is/am/are + being + past participle.

questions.text: Choose the correct passive voice: 'He has finished his work.'
options: His work is finished by him.
His work was finished by him.
His work had been finished by him.
His work has been finished by him.
questions.explanation: The present perfect passive is formed with has/have been + past participle.

questions.text: Choose the correct passive voice: 'The teacher was teaching the students.'
options: The students were being taught by the teacher.
The students are being taught by the teacher.
The students had been taught by the teacher.
The students were taught by the teacher.
questions.explanation: The past continuous passive is formed with was/were + being + past participle.

questions.text: Choose the correct passive voice: 'They had completed the task before I arrived.'
options: The task was completed by them before I arrived.
The task had been completed by them before I arrived.
The task has been completed by them before I arrived.
The task is completed by them before I arrived.
questions.explanation: The past perfect passive is formed with had been + past participle.

questions.text: Choose the correct passive voice: 'You must obey the rules.'
options: The rules are obeyed by you.
The rules must be obeyed by you.
The rules should be obeyed by you.
questions.explanation: With modal verbs, the passive is formed as modal + be + past participle, keeping the original modal.

questions.text: Choose the correct passive voice: 'Open the door.'
questions.explanation: Imperative sentences are made passive using "Let + object + be + past participle."

questions.text: Choose the correct passive voice: 'Who wrote this novel?'
options: By whom was this novel written?
By whom this novel was written?
By whom is this novel written?
questions.explanation: In passive questions with "wh-" words, the auxiliary comes before the subject: "By whom was this novel written?"

questions.text: Choose the correct passive voice: 'She teaches us English.'
options: English is taught to us by her.
We are taught English by her.
We are taught by English her.
English is taught us by her.
questions.explanation: With verbs that take two objects, the indirect object usually becomes the subject of the passive: "We are taught English by her."

questions.text: Choose the correct passive voice: 'People speak English all over the world.'
options: English is spoken by people all over the world.
English was spoken all over the world.
English is spoken all over the world.
English has been spoken all over the world.
questions.explanation: When the agent is a vague or general word such as "people", it is dropped in the passive.

questions.text: Choose the correct passive voice: 'The manager will have signed the contract by Friday.'
options: The contract will be signed by the manager by Friday.
The contract is signed by the manager by Friday.
The contract had been signed by the manager by Friday.
The contract will have been signed by the manager by Friday.
questions.explanation: The future perfect passive is formed with will have been + past participle.

questions.text: Choose the correct passive voice: 'Someone has stolen my bicycle.'
options: My bicycle was stolen by someone.
My bicycle is stolen by someone.
My bicycle had been stolen by someone.
questions.explanation: When the doer is unknown, as with "someone", the agent phrase is usually omitted in the passive.

questions.text: Choose the correct passive voice: 'They are building a new bridge.'
options: A new bridge is built by them.
A new bridge is being built by them.
A new bridge was being built by them.
A new bridge has been built by them.
questions.explanation: The present continuous passive is formed with is/am/are + being + past participle.

questions.text: Choose the correct passive voice: 'I saw him crossing the road.'
options: He was seen crossing by me the road.
He is seen crossing the road by me.
He was seen crossing the road by me.
He had been seen crossing the road by me.
questions.explanation: The passive of "saw + object + present participle" retains the participle: "He was seen crossing the road by me."

questions.text: Choose the correct passive voice: 'Please close the window.'
options: You are requested to close the window.
questions.explanation: A polite imperative is usually rendered in the passive as "You are requested to..."

questions.text: Choose the correct passive voice: 'They elected him president.'
options: He was elected president by them.
He is elected president by them.
He was elected as president by they.
questions.explanation: The object complement "president" is retained after the verb in the passive.

questions.text: Choose the correct passive voice: 'We should finish this work today.'
options: This work is finished by us today.
This work should be finished by us today.
This work should finish by us today.
This work will be finished by us today.
questions.explanation: Modal passive: should + be + past participle, keeping the original modal verb.

questions.text: Choose the correct passive voice: 'The chairman will inaugurate the new building.'
options: The new building is inaugurated by the chairman.
The new building was inaugurated by the chairman.
The new building will be inaugurated by the chairman.
The new building will inaugurate by the chairman.
questions.explanation: Simple future passive is formed with will be + past participle.

questions.text: Choose the correct passive voice: 'She had written the letter before he came.'
options: The letter was written by her before he came.
The letter has been written by her before he came.
The letter is written by her before he came.
The letter had been written by her before he came.
questions.explanation: The past perfect passive is formed with had been + past participle.

questions.text: Choose the correct passive voice: 'Do not waste time.'
questions.explanation: Negative imperatives are made passive using "Let + object + not + be + past participle."

questions.text: Choose the correct passive voice: 'He is repairing the car.'
options: The car is repaired by him.
The car is being repaired by him.
The car was being repaired by him.
The car has been repaired by him.
questions.explanation: The present continuous passive is formed with is/am/are + being + past participle.

questions.text: Choose the correct passive voice: 'The workers were digging the trench.'
options: The trench is dug by the workers.
The trench was dug by the workers.
The trench was being dug by the workers.
The trench has been dug by the workers.
questions.explanation: The past continuous passive is formed with was/were + being + past participle.

questions.text: Choose the correct passive voice: 'The judge will have delivered the verdict by noon.'
options: The verdict will be delivered by the judge by noon.
The verdict is delivered by the judge by noon.
The verdict had been delivered by the judge by noon.
The verdict will have been delivered by the judge by noon.
questions.explanation: The future perfect passive is formed with will have been + past participle.

questions.text: Convert to indirect speech: He said, 'I am going to school.'
options: He said that he was going to school.
He said that he is going to school.
He told that he was going to school.
He said that he had gone to school.
questions.explanation: A present tense in direct speech shifts to the past tense in indirect speech when the reporting verb is in the past.

questions.text: Convert to indirect speech: She said, 'I have finished my homework.'
options: She said that she finished her homework.
She said that she had finished her homework.
She said that she has finished her homework.
She told that she had finished her homework.
questions.explanation: The present perfect in direct speech becomes the past perfect in indirect speech.

questions.text: Convert to indirect speech: He said to me, 'I will help you.'
options: He told me that he would help me.
He said to me that he will help me.
He told me that he will help me.
He said that he would help you.
questions.explanation: "Said to" becomes "told" before a personal object, and "will" shifts to "would" in past reporting.

questions.text: Convert to indirect speech: The teacher said to the students, 'Work hard.'
options: The teacher said the students to work hard.
The teacher told the students that work hard.
The teacher ordered the students working hard.
The teacher told the students to work hard.
questions.explanation: Imperative sentences in indirect speech use an infinitive: "told + object + to + verb."

questions.text: Convert to indirect speech: She said, 'Please help me.'
options: She requested me to help her.
She told me please help her.
questions.explanation: A polite request introduced by "please" is reported using "requested."

questions.text: Convert to indirect speech: He said, 'Do not make noise.'
options: He said to not make noise.
He told them not to make noise.
He told them to not making noise.
He said that do not make noise.
questions.explanation: Negative imperatives are reported using "told + object + not + to + verb."

questions.text: Convert to indirect speech: She said, 'What is your name?'
options: She asked what was my name.
She asked what my name is.
She asked what my name was.
She asked that what my name was.
questions.explanation: In reported questions, subject-verb order is restored, the tense shifts back, and no "that" or question mark is used.

questions.text: Convert to indirect speech: He said, 'Where do you live?'
options: He asked where did I live.
He asked that where I lived.
questions.explanation: The auxiliary "do" disappears and the question word introduces a statement-order clause with the tense shifted back.

questions.text: Convert to indirect speech: She said, 'Did you complete the work?'
options: She asked whether I had completed the work.
She asked did I complete the work.
She asked that I had completed the work.
She asked whether I completed the work.
questions.explanation: Yes/no questions are reported using "if/whether", with the tense shifted back to the past perfect.

questions.text: Convert to indirect speech: He said, 'How beautiful the sunset is!'
options: He said how beautiful the sunset was.
He exclaimed that the sunset was very beautiful.
He exclaimed how beautiful is the sunset.
He exclaimed that how beautiful the sunset was.
questions.explanation: Exclamatory sentences are reported using "exclaimed that", converting the exclamation into a statement of degree.

questions.text: Convert to indirect speech: She said, 'Alas! I have failed.'
options: She said alas that she had failed.
She exclaimed alas that she had failed.
She exclaimed with sorrow that she had failed.
She exclaimed that she has failed.
questions.explanation: An interjection such as "Alas!" is replaced with a phrase naming the emotion, such as "with sorrow."

questions.text: Convert to indirect speech: He said, 'Let us go for a walk.'
options: He said that let us go for a walk.
He told us to go for a walk.
He suggested going for a walk.
He proposed that they should go for a walk.
questions.explanation: "Let us" proposals are reported with "proposed/suggested that + subject + should + verb."

questions.text: Convert to indirect speech: The boy said, 'I saw the accident yesterday.'
options: The boy said that he had seen the accident the previous day.
The boy said that he saw the accident yesterday.
The boy said that he had seen the accident yesterday.
The boy said that he has seen the accident the previous day.
questions.explanation: "Yesterday" changes to "the previous day" and the simple past shifts to the past perfect when the reporting verb is in the past.

questions.text: Convert to indirect speech: She said, 'I am writing a letter now.'
options: She said that she is writing a letter now.
She said that she was writing a letter then.
She said that she was writing a letter now.
She said that she had been writing a letter then.
questions.explanation: "Now" changes to "then" and the present continuous shifts to the past continuous in indirect speech.

questions.text: Convert to indirect speech: He said, 'I shall come here tomorrow.'
options: He said that he would come here tomorrow.
He said that he would come there the next day.
He said that he would go there the next day.
He said that he will go there the next day.
questions.explanation: "Come" changes to "go", "here" to "there", and "tomorrow" to "the next day" when the place and time of reporting differ from those of speaking.

questions.text: Convert to indirect speech: She said to me, 'I can help you with this.'
options: She told me that she can help me with that.
She told me that she could help me with this.
She told me that I could help her with that.
She told me that she could help me with that.
questions.explanation: "Can" shifts to "could", and "this" shifts to "that" in indirect speech.

questions.text: Convert to indirect speech: He said, 'I must finish this work today.'
options: He said that he had to finish that work that day.
He said that he must finish this work today.
He said that he had to finish this work today.
He said that he must finished that work that day.
questions.explanation: "Must" expressing obligation is generally reported as "had to", with "this" and "today" also shifting.

questions.text: Convert to indirect speech: The teacher said, 'The earth revolves around the sun.'
options: The teacher said that the earth revolved around the sun.
The teacher said that the earth revolves around the sun.
The teacher told that the earth revolves around the sun.
The teacher said the earth revolves around the sun.
questions.explanation: A universal truth keeps its original tense even when the reporting verb is in the past.

questions.text: Convert to indirect speech: He said, 'I was ill yesterday.'
options: He said that he was ill the previous day.
He said that he is ill the previous day.
He said that he had been ill the previous day.
He said that he had been ill yesterday.
questions.explanation: A simple past tense in direct speech shifts to the past perfect in indirect speech, and "yesterday" changes to "the previous day."

questions.text: Convert to indirect speech: She said, 'May you live long!'
options: She said that I may live long.
She wished that I live long.
She hoped I will live long.
She prayed that I might live long.
questions.explanation: Blessings introduced by "May" are reported using "prayed/wished that + subject + might."

questions.text: Convert to indirect speech: She said, 'I have never been to London.'
options: She said that she had never been to London.
She said that she has never been to London.
She said that she never was to London.
She said that she never been to London.
questions.explanation: The present perfect shifts to the past perfect in indirect speech.

questions.text: Convert to indirect speech: The captain said to the soldiers, 'March forward.'
options: The captain said to the soldiers to march forward.
The captain ordered the soldiers to march forward.
The captain told the soldiers that march forward.
The captain ordered the soldiers marching forward.
questions.explanation: A command from a person in authority is reported using "ordered + object + to + verb."

questions.text: Convert to indirect speech: He said, 'Shall I open the window?'
options: He asked if he shall open the window.
He asked that he should open the window.
He asked if he should open the window.
He asked whether he shall open the window.
questions.explanation: "Shall I", offering to do something, is reported using "should" in indirect speech.

questions.text: Convert to indirect speech: She said, 'Let me think about it.'
options: She said that let her think about it.
She suggested that she think about it.
She told me to think about it.
She said that she would think about it.
questions.explanation: "Let me", expressing a self-directed intention, is reported as "would" plus the base verb.

questions.text: Convert to indirect speech: He said, 'I bought this car last week.'
options: He said that he had bought that car the previous week.
He said that he bought that car last week.
He said that he had bought this car last week.
He said that he has bought that car the previous week.
questions.explanation: The simple past shifts to the past perfect, and "this/last week" shift to "that/the previous week" in indirect speech.

questions.text: Which sentence correctly punctuates the non-restrictive clause?
options: My brother who lives in Karachi is a doctor.
My brother, who lives in Karachi, is a doctor.
My brother, who lives in Karachi is a doctor.
My brother who lives in Karachi, is a doctor.
questions.explanation: A non-restrictive relative clause giving extra, non-essential information is set off by commas on both sides.

questions.text: Which sentence uses the apostrophe correctly?
options: The boys books were left on the table.
The boy's book's were left on the table.
The boys' books were left on the table.
The boys's books were left on the table.
questions.explanation: For a plural noun already ending in "s", the possessive is formed by adding only an apostrophe after the "s."

questions.text: Which of the following words is a proper noun that must always be capitalised?
questions.explanation: Proper nouns such as "Everest" (a specific named mountain) are always capitalised; common nouns like "summer", "college", and "river" are not.

questions.text: Which sentence uses the semicolon correctly?
options: I wanted to go for a walk; it started raining.
I wanted to go for a walk; but it started raining.
I wanted to go for a walk, it started raining.
I wanted to go for a walk: it started raining.
questions.explanation: A semicolon joins two closely related independent clauses without a coordinating conjunction such as "but."

questions.text: Which sentence uses the colon correctly?
options: She bought: apples, oranges, and bananas.
She bought the following fruits: apples, oranges, and bananas.
She bought the following fruits, apples, oranges, and bananas.
She bought the following fruits; apples, oranges, and bananas.
questions.explanation: A colon is used after a complete independent clause to introduce a list.

questions.text: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
questions.explanation: The question mark belongs inside the closing quotation mark when it punctuates the quoted question itself.

questions.text: Which sentence correctly reports an indirect question?
options: He asked what time it was?
He asked, what time it was.
He asked what time was it.
He asked what time it was.
questions.explanation: An indirect question is a statement in form and ends with a full stop, not a question mark, and follows normal word order.

questions.text: Which of these should be capitalised whenever it appears in a sentence?
questions.explanation: "Urdu" is the name of a language, a proper noun, and is always capitalised; "college", "subject", and "notebook" are common nouns.

questions.text: Which sentence uses the hyphen correctly?
options: He gave a well known lecture on economics.
He gave a well-known lecture on economics.
He gave a well-known-lecture on economics.
He gave a well, known lecture on economics.
questions.explanation: A compound adjective placed before a noun, such as "well-known", is hyphenated.

questions.text: Which sentence correctly punctuates the list of items?
options: I bought pens pencils, and notebooks for school.
I bought pens, pencils and, notebooks for school.
I bought pens, pencils, and notebooks for school.
I bought pens, pencils notebooks, for school.
questions.explanation: Items in a series are separated by commas, with a comma before the final conjunction.

questions.text: Which sentence correctly uses a comma after an introductory phrase?
options: After finishing his homework he went to play.
After finishing his homework, went to play he.
After finishing, his homework he went to play.
After finishing his homework, he went to play.
questions.explanation: A comma follows an introductory phrase or clause before the main clause begins.

questions.text: Which sentence uses quotation marks and punctuation correctly?
options: The teacher said, "Read the chapter carefully."
The teacher said "Read the chapter carefully."
The teacher said, "Read the chapter carefully".
The teacher said "Read the chapter carefully".
questions.explanation: A comma introduces the quoted speech, and the closing punctuation is placed inside the final quotation mark.

questions.text: In the title "The Old Man and the Sea," why does the second "the" stay lowercase?
options: Because articles are never capitalised in titles
Because it is a minor word and not the first word of the title
questions.explanation: In title case, minor words such as articles, short prepositions, and conjunctions stay lowercase unless they open or close the title; the leading "The" is capitalised but the second "the" before "Sea" is not.

questions.text: Which sentence correctly punctuates a direct address?
questions.explanation: A noun of direct address is set off from the rest of the sentence by a comma.

questions.text: Which sentence correctly distinguishes 'its' from 'it's'?
options: Its important to submit the form before it's deadline.
Its important to submit the form before its' deadline.
It's important to submit the form before it's deadline.
It's important to submit the form before its deadline.
questions.explanation: "It's" is the contraction of "it is", while "its" is the possessive form; the sentence needs "It's important" and "its deadline."

questions.text: One word for 'a person who studies and is skilled in the science of birds':
questions.explanation: An ornithologist specialises in the scientific study of birds.

questions.text: One word for 'a person who can speak two languages':
questions.explanation: "Bilingual" specifically means able to speak two languages, whereas "polyglot" means able to speak many languages.

questions.text: One word for 'a place where birds are kept':
questions.explanation: An aviary is a large enclosure built for keeping birds.

questions.text: One word for 'one who loves and works for the welfare of mankind':
questions.explanation: A philanthropist devotes wealth or effort to promoting human welfare.

questions.text: One word for 'a person who hates mankind':
questions.explanation: A misanthrope is someone who dislikes or distrusts humankind in general.

questions.text: One word for 'a person who walks in his sleep':
questions.explanation: A somnambulist is a person who walks about while asleep.

questions.text: One word for 'a person who is one hundred years old or more':
questions.explanation: A centenarian is a person who has reached the age of one hundred.

questions.text: One word for 'a list of books referred to in a piece of writing':
questions.explanation: A bibliography is a list of sources or books used or cited in a work.

questions.text: One word for 'the scientific study of insects':
questions.explanation: Entomology is the branch of zoology dealing with insects; it should not be confused with "etymology", the study of word origins.

questions.text: One word for 'a word, phrase, or sentence that reads the same backward as forward':
questions.explanation: A palindrome, such as "madam", reads identically in both directions.

questions.text: One word for 'a person who knows everything':
questions.explanation: "Omniscient" means having complete or infinite knowledge.

questions.text: One word for 'government by a small, privileged group of people':
questions.explanation: An oligarchy is rule by a small group of people, often for their own interests.

questions.text: One word for 'a person who compiles or writes a dictionary':
questions.explanation: A lexicographer is a person who compiles dictionaries.

questions.text: One word for 'an abnormal fear of enclosed or confined spaces':
questions.explanation: Claustrophobia is an intense fear of confined spaces.

questions.text: One word for 'the life history of a person written by himself':
questions.explanation: An autobiography is a self-written account of one's own life.
